segments.narration: Red-Black Trees. Self-balancing binary search trees that guarantee logarithmic time for every operation.

A Red-Black Tree is a self-balancing BST where each node stores an extra bit representing color: red or black. The tree maintains balance through a set of invariants that ensure no path is more than twice as long as any other.
Think of it as a tree that trims its own branches. After every insertion or deletion, it checks if it got lopsided, then recolors nodes and rotates to restore balance.

Five rules govern the tree. One: every node is either red or black. Two: the root is always black. Three: all leaves, which are NIL nodes, are black. Four: if a node is red, both children are black, no two reds in a row. Five: every path from a node to its descendant leaves contains the same number of black nodes.
Insertion works in three phases. First, insert like a normal BST and color the new node red. Second, fix violations by recoloring and rotating. Third, ensure the root ends black.

Search, insert, and delete all run in order log n time. Space complexity is order n. This is identical to AVL trees for search, but Red-Black trees are faster for insertions and deletions because they require fewer rotations.

Pros: guaranteed balance, efficient for frequent insertions and deletions, used in real systems like the Linux kernel rbtree and C++ map. Cons: more complex to implement than a basic BST, slightly less strictly balanced than AVL, which can mean marginally slower lookups.

Use Red-Black trees when you need ordered data with guaranteed performance, especially when insertions and deletions are frequent. Linux uses them for process scheduling. Java's TreeMap and C++ std map are Red-Black trees under the hood.
Here's a mnemonic to remember the rules. Every red node has two black nephews. The root is always dressed in black. All paths to the leaves have equal black depth.
Cheat sheet. Red-Black tree. Time: log n for all ops. Space: order n. Invariants: five rules. Rotations: left and right. Used in: Linux kernel, C++ map, Java TreeMap.
That's Red-Black Trees. If this helped, check out the AVL Tree video next to compare the two approaches.
